analytic.title: An Architecture to Enable Machine-Learning-Based Task Migration for Multi-Core Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: ECU consolidation is an automotive trend that tends to reduce the number of electronic devices in a vehicle to optimize resources and costs. However, its implementation introduces new challenges, especially in terms of safety. Research at our group is exploring the idea of task migration between different electronic-control-units (ECUs) to add redundancy and fail-safety capabilities to an automotive setup. In particular, we are exploring machine-learning-aided schedulability analysis strategies as means to decide which ECU a task should be mapped to. In this paper. we present the implementation of an architecture that allows for testing different machine-learning techniques for schedulability analysis, enabling the deployment of tasks to the respective ECUs and a simple migration of tasks between them. The architecture is based on a real-time operating system. The test system developed implements a mix of dummy tasks with constant execution times and an autonomous task that interacts with a virtual environment and with a variable execution time. Also, the architecture allows for collecting data on each task for proving if the executed task sets are actually schedulable, as predicted by the machine learning component.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The future of the automotive industry is being greatly shaped by the introduction of computer-based technologies, with the general goals of increasing user comfort and safety [1]. This results in a vast majority of innovations in the industry being driven by electronic related developments [2]. These developments contribute to a constant increase in the computational requirements of modern cars and are, therefore, an additional optimization factor in an industry where resource efficiency is of great importance. As the contribution of electronics to car costs are accounting for more than one third of their total [2], automotive manufacturers need to search for ways of optimizing the usage of computational resources.

Modern cars include dozens of electronic control units (ECUs), a number likely to increase considering past trends of adding lots of single-purpose devices to fulfill new computational tasks in the vehicle [3], [4]. This development is, however, unsustainable and presents problems in terms of power, cost and weight efficiency [1], [4]. ECU consolidation aims to solve these issues by executing tasks on a few This work was partially funded by the European Union (EU) under RIA grant n°825050 powerful, multiple-purpose devices, but this approach comes with challenges in maximizing the efficiency of the system, ensuring all tasks get to execute and meet their deadlines and deciding which device each task should be allocated to.

Research at our group has explored dynamic task migration as a method for enabling ECU consolidation. This migration would allow moving tasks from one device to another, depending on some conditions, such as the utilization and availability of the devices and the firing and completion of the tasks. To achieve this, the migration process is divided in two stages: the planning, which maps the tasks to the ECUs that will execute them; and the execution, which allows for moving tasks to a different ECU if needed.

The idea of task migration in our research considers the possibility of using machine learning techniques to plan the distribution of tasks to different devices, which are applied to perform a prediction on the schedulability analysis for such distributions. This is motivated by the fact that traditional methods, though normally able to ensure the feasibility of a schedule, are often pessimistic and perform recurrent calculations [5], which gets very complex and computation-heavy for larger task sets or when introducing complex function calls that introduce additional constraints like resource sharing or dependency. In contrast the machine-learning techniques explored at our research group have shown the potential of providing a highly accurate and fast prediction of the feasibility of a task set. Additionally, machine learning techniques allow for predicting even in the presence of uncertainties in the execution, as might happen when interaction with the real world is considered, which might cause some automotive tasks to have variable execution times.

One of the challenges this strategy faces is the fact that realtime constraints have to be met, as automotive tasks are often safety critical. For this reason, investigating the integration of the machine-learning techniques with real-time platforms used in the automotive industry and with realistic conditions is necessary for evaluation of the different strategies. In this paper, we present an architecture to enable a simple distribution of a set of real-time tasks to a set of ECUs and which is capable of adapting to new task distributions in real time, as well as providing feedback information for the machine learning. To show these capabilities, a hardware-in-the-loop setup was developed, which allows for testing different migration planning strategies with different types of real-time tasks.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II presents related work concerning the idea of task migration, especially in the automotive environment. Section III presents the embedded system used as a development platform and the setup used for testing the approach. Section IV gives a brief overview of the tasks used to test the approach. Section V explains the approach used in the operating system to achieve the dynamic task allocation as decided in the planning phase. The analysis of the system and the results obtained from the implementation and test of the architecture are presented in section VI and then discussed in section VII. Finally, conclusions are drawn and future work is mentioned in section VIII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The idea of task migration has been explored in research as an approach to enable distributed systems to execute a wider variety of tasks. In the case of our research, this idea is applied to real-time systems, aiming to enable ECU consolidation. Some authors have explored the concept in the form of developing different scheduling strategies, such as in [6], [7]. These examples, however, have not focused on the implementation of a system capable of scheduling and executing the task migration, and rather compare the performance of their strategy with more known ones, such as earliest-deadline-first (EDF). In the regard of implementing a migration of tasks between ECUs, Chen and Lyu have explored the creation of a framework for FlexRay systems, where a backup device (called node in their work) is always ready to take over the tasks of a failing one [8]. Their approach differs from the one presented here because we explore the idea of migrating tasks separately and between already running devices, while theirs moved all tasks from the device with a failure to the backup one.

The idea of applying machine learning methods to solve the challenges of schedulability analysis, especially its mathematical complexity when using traditional methods, has been analyzed previously by researchers in several disciplines. While older approaches have investigated the usage of neural networks for performing the schedulability analysis at the design stage of the system, they did not explore the applications for deploying tasks in real time [9], [10]. More recent developments have explored the usage of different machine learning techniques, such as reinforcement learning and shallow learning, to distribute tasks among several components [11], [12]. However, the idea of online task migration with the usage of machine learning has not been widely explored, and the most similar use case we know of is a distributed system that allows tasks to be offloaded to cloud resources, whereas the research in our group explores the usage in automotive real-time systems [13].

KIA4SM [14], a previous project at our research group, investigated the creation of an architecture that would enable task migration. The contributions of KIA4SM include the development of a generic architecture that allows the migration of tasks to different kinds of hardware in an automotive network, as well as exploring the usage of machine learning for planning the distribution of tasks in the network and a checkpoint-restore mechanism for migrating tasks between devices. From this project, a variety of internal research projects have originated, exploring the usage of different machine learning techniques and task deployment tools. The ideas in KIA4SM and subsequent work at the chair, however, were developed on different platforms and operating systems, with less focus on a real-time implementation of the migration. Additionally, the setup in KIA4SM served as an inspiration for the one used in this work to test the developments.

div.head: A. ECU System
div.p: The system developed as the target ECUs consists of an ARM-based development board, containing a Xilinx Ultra-Scale+ MPSoC. This MPSoC contains two processors: an ARM Cortex-A53 with 4 cores, and an ARM Cortex-R5 with 2 cores, of which only core 0 of the A53 was used for this work, but an extension to all cores of the processor is planned for the near future. This selection of hardware was applied to all the devices used as ECUs.

FreeRTOS was selected as operating system, as its features allow for testing the capabilities of the approach: it offers the possibility of implementing real-time capabilities, such as priority-based preemptive scheduling, measuring execution times and triggering time-based events with relatively good precision. Additionally, the popularity of FreeRTOS in the industry, its tiny kernel and the availability of open-source libraries further motivated this decision.

To test the distribution of the tasks, a set of tasks were developed. These tasks are meant to allow for achieving a high system utilization, but also allow for testing with a range of different worst case execution times, periods, and also including a simulated autonomous task. Details on the executed tasks are explained in the next section.

div.head: B. Test Setup
div.p: The test setup, depicted in figure 1, consists mainly of the following elements: a machine-learning-based schedulability analysis algorithm, which predicts if a task distribution will be able to execute correctly; a task deployment tool, which generates task distributions, triggers their schedulability prediction and deploys the best predicted distribution to the devices; and the devices executing the tasks according to the task distribution.

The devices communicate with the deployment tool by means of a task that receives the respective distributed task set, and sends back the information on whether the task set was executed successfully or if any deadlines were missed. The deployment task at the devices is then responsible for starting and stopping the tasks and monitoring their status.

The task deployment tool is the center of the setup, as it communicates directly with the devices and triggers the execution of the tasks. This communication allows for executing tasks with a certain or unlimited number of jobs, and it is explained further in the next sections. This tool is also responsible for detecting failures on the embedded devices, and for generating new task distributions, predicting new feasible distributions with the previously trained machine learning model if the active distribution misses at least one deadline (that is, it is deemed as unschedulable), and performing online training with the results reported by the devices on whether the task set was successfully executed. Additionally, the deployment tool allows for testing with different schedulability analysis algorithms by changing the machine learning model component.

The setup allows for testing different machine learning algorithms in the prediction phase, however the work presented here was only tested extensively with a spiking neural network (SNN) running on a SpiNNaker neuromorphic hardware. This means that the machine learning runs on a dedicated hardware, allowing the ECUs to be dedicated fully to the real-time tasks. Even if we only introduce the SNN as a use case in this paper, the setup and the work described in this paper allow for comparing the performance of the different machine-learning algorithms for the deployment of task sets with challenging constraints to a set of ECUs, which is planned to be presented in future publications.

div.head: IV. TASKS
div.p: There are two types of tasks in our development: dummy tasks, which are automatically generated and are used to fill the utilization of the ECUs and test the system under different conditions; and one simulated autonomous task, which allows for testing the system under a realistic use-case, showing failures in a graphical environment and also introducing variability in the execution times. Both are explained below. For the sake of simplicity, all tasks in this work are periodic with relative deadlines equal to their respective periods. Additionally, they may have a defined number of jobs to be executed or execute indefinitely unless the task distribution changes, and they may be started or stopped at any time.

div.head: A. Dummy Tasks
div.p: To automatically generate tasks, the task set generator from the COBRA framework, developed at the University of Antwerp, was used [15]. This tool chain creates tasks with random execution times and periods until a certain total utilization value is filled. It then uses a set of programs from TACLeBench [16] and a mathematical solver to find a combination of said programs that will have an execution time virtually equal to the one previously generated for the task. In order to use the tools in the COBRA framework in this work, it was necessary to extend it for working on an ARM64 architecture and producing FreeRTOS compatible code.

By extending the COBRA framework, it was possible to automatically generate tasks with pseudo-random execution times and periods in a range of 100 ms to 10 s. This allowed for testing the system with tasks with a wide variety of utilization values and a total utilization approaching 100% of all devices. Additionally, as the programs in TACLeBench (which COBRA uses to produce the tasks) use shared resources, the usage of these tasks introduced an additional challenge to the development, as often tasks had to be preempted. This was solved by using mutexes and wrapping the TACLeBench program calls in functions that took the mutex for their proper execution.

A limitation in the extensions to COBRA in this work exists, as the original framework is based on formal calculation of the cycles necessary for executing the TACLeBench programs in the target architecture, and this was not performed in the scope of this paper. Instead, to make the COBRA framework produce relevant tasks, the worst case execution time of the TACLeBench programs on the ARM64 architecture was estimated by performing end-to-end measurements over large numbers of runs for each program and averaging their execution times. This measurement might be very inaccurate for single executions of the programs, but for the purpose of this work it showed to work fine, as the combined execution times were good enough to produce meaningful predictions using the machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, an exact worst-case-execution-time analysis is usually time consuming, and we assume its advantages might be overcome by the predictions from the machine learning.

div.head: B. Autonomous Task
div.p: The autonomous task developed had the goal of making a robot find the exit of a labyrinth in the simulation, which communicated with the ECU via UDP exchanging sensor and control data. For this to work, this task was divided in two subtasks: one that communicated with the simulation to receive sensor data and send control signals, and another that used simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) to explore the surroundings based on the received sensor data and generated the control output. Both sub-tasks communicated by means of a shared memory block.

The SLAM sub-task was based on TinySLAM [17], a simple algorithm that allows to create a map and estimate the position of an object based on a single LIDAR scan, which was received in the communication sub-task and written on the shared-memory block. The created map contains certainty values for whether a certain position has an obstacle or is free, so unexplored positions are uncertain. This information was used to find the nearest unexplored position to the robot and calculate the needed angular and linear velocity for reaching that position, taking obstacles into account. Afterwards, these velocities were written on the shared-memory block and sent back to the simulation.

The addition of this task allowed to show in the simulation when the ECU executing it was having trouble to meet the deadlines, as the control would become slow and the robot would often crash into obstacles in the labyrinth. It also helped find shortcomings in the migration strategy, as the created map was stored locally, and so changing the hardware to which the autonomous task was mapped to meant losing the exploration progress, as no mechanism for migrating the task context, such as checkpoint-restore, was implemented in the scope of this work.

An important aspect in this task, as opposed to the dummy tasks, is that its execution time may vary greatly, depending on whether sensor data have been received and on how far the search for an unexplored position goes, as these uncertainties come from the environment. In fact, using end-to-endmeasurement, the worst-case-execution-time for this task was found to be around 550 ms, while the average execution time was only around 210 ms. This condition is assumed to be beneficial for our research as it allows for handling tasks with large variation in their execution times in the machine learning algorithm.

div.head: V. TASK DEPLOYMENT AND EXECUTION
div.p: To enable the deployment of the tasks from the task deployment tool, a few extensions to the basic FreeRTOS functionality were implemented on the ECUs. First, the addition of a scheduler which allowed for achieving the highest utilization possible of the devices was introduced. Then, a task was added for receiving the deployed task distributions, starting the execution of the tasks, monitoring their status and sending back to the central deployment tool.

div.head: A. Scheduler
div.p: While the machine learning component could be adapted to any scheduling policy, it is relevant to test the approach on a system with real-time scheduling. That means that timing constraints are considered for the selection of a suitable policy. In this case, we consider the worst-case execution time C i , period T i and relative deadline D i of a given task τ i as the relevant values. As in this work only periodic tasks with relative deadlines equal to their periods are explored, we can assume that D i = T i . Additionally, we use the concept of processor utilization U , where U i = Ci Ti denotes the utilization corresponding to task τ i and U = n i=1 U i for a task set containing n tasks.

Let us consider two of the most commonly used scheduling policies in real-time systems: rate-monotonic (RM), which assigns fixed priorities to the tasks, and earliest-deadline-first (EDF), which uses dynamic priorities.

Rate-monotonic scheduling assigns higher priority to tasks with shorter periods. In the case of preemptive scheduling, this policy is optimal among fixed-priority schedulers, meaning that it will always find a feasible schedule for a task set if it exists [5]. In [5], it is demonstrated that a task set will be feasible under RM scheduling if
div.formula: n i=1 C i T i ≤ n(2 1/n -1)
div.p: This value is always smaller than 1 for n > 1, and it tends to a lower bound of U = ln2 for increasing n. This test is somewhat pessimistic, but it shows that the maximal utilization of an optimal fixed-priority strategy is not the highest for large numbers of tasks. This is compared to a dynamic-priority strategy next.

In the case of the earliest-deadline-first scheduler, priority is assigned to each job separately according to its deadline, meaning that the job with the most urgent deadline is executed first. This, in addition to a preemptive strategy, allows the policy to be optimal among all schedulers [18]. Actually, it is shown in [5] that for a given task set on a single processor, there will be a feasible schedule if and only if
div.formula: n i=1 C i T i ≤ 1
div.p: which means that all task sets that are schedulable under a RM policy are also schedulable under an EDF policy.

These formulas apply only if implementation overhead for handling the dynamic policies and context switches are neglected. However, as shown in [19], a preemptive EDF scheduler also tends to enforce less context switches than a preemptive RM scheduler, making up for less implementation overhead, even with the dynamic priority assignation. Furthermore, as the schedulability analysis is performed by the machine learning component, we assumed that the uncertainties introduced by the implementation overhead can be taken into account by using a rich data set. For these reasons, to ensure the highest utilization possible in the devices while meeting all deadlines if possible, a preemptive earliest-deadline-first (EDF) scheduler was chosen.

To achieve this, the ESFREE open-source library was used [20]. This is because FreeRTOS does not offer implemented priority policies, and ESFREE extends the basic scheduler to add these policies and assign dynamic priorities to the tasks. Its integration allowed for testing periodic tasks executing indefinitely, but it was extended to allow the dynamic creation and deletion of tasks, and with a certain number of jobs, as required by the deployment tool. Additionally, the scheduler was extended to report the status of the executed tasks, that is, whether the task is currently executing, as well as the number of jobs executed and the number of deadlines missed.

The EDF scheduler was used for executing all the deployed tasks (both the dummy tasks and the autonomous task). However, higher priority tasks, such as the communication tasks and the deployment tasks, were scheduled using a fixed priority, higher than the ones the EDF scheduler could assign.

div.head: B. Deployment Task
div.p: The deployment task in the ECUs was divided in two sub-tasks: the communication, responsible for receiving the task distribution from the deployment tool and sending back the status of the currently executed tasks; and the monitor, which started the received tasks and constantly checked their status. As these sub-tasks were not scheduled using the EDF policy, they executed at a high priority and with a medium fixed period (every second), these allowed for communicating continuously with the deployment tool, while still leaving most of the processing power for the other tasks. Both sub-tasks communicate with each other by means of a shared memory block.

The communication with the deployment tool occurs via TCP, exchanging JSON messages. The information received from the tool includes the ID of the ECU that should execute the sent task set, as well as an instruction (whether the tasks should be added to a running task distribution, a new distribution should be started, a distribution should be deleted, etc.) and an array with the information of the tasks corresponding to that instruction. The information on the tasks deployed to a board include an ID number for the given task, the number of jobs to be executed for this task (or whether the task should execute indefinitely), and real-time relevant information: worst-case execution time for the task, relative deadline and period. The communication sub-task then creates a list of task objects based on the received data, which the monitor sub-task will then start. If tasks need to be deleted, the communication thread does so, as this should be performed before the list is updated. The information sent back contains the current status of the ECU (whether it is idle, running tasks, has missed a deadline or has finished running all tasks successfully), as well as an array with the status for every task.

The monitor sub-task first checks for new tasks in the list, then starts them in the EDF scheduler. Afterwards, it checks periodically every task in the list for the number of jobs executed, missed deadlines and completion status. This information is then used to fill the data that is sent back to the deployment tool.

In this stage, it is important to note that for this implementation, the delay introduced by the communication and starting process of the tasks was neglected. This would mean that an unknown phase φ i is introduced for every task τ i . The effects of this shortcoming are considered minor at this stage of our research, but they would have a large impact on a final system, and they include an uncertain delay in the deadlines of the tasks and possible changes in the schedulability of particular task sets, where the phase might change the result.

div.head: VI. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
div.p: The analysis of the system developed in this paper was carried out in two stages: first, only its ability to execute a deployed task set and send the execution back was tested, and then its integration with the task deployment tool and the machine learning components. In this section, these stages are described and the results gathered on the implementation of the system are shown briefly.

For performing the initial stage of the analysis, random task sets containing any subset of the developed tasks were generated and executed on the embedded boards, letting every task set run for around one minute. Then the relevant runtime information was collected and structured into initial training and test data sets. The information contained in the data set is comprised of previously known values, such as the number of tasks, task periods, WCETs and deadlines (which are used input values), as well as the newly gathered information on the number of missed deadlines and successful jobs for each task (used as training labels). The data set generated is still small, comprising of only several thousands of samples, but contains the information necessary to generate a prediction on the probability of the schedulability of a deployed task set.

As mentioned earlier, in this paper the machine learning component of the deployment tool was equipped with a spiking neural network running on a SpiNNaker. The SNN developed was a very simple one, consisting of only an input and an output population of neurons, connected in an allto-all fashion with STDP (spike-timing-dependent plasticity) synapses and using rate coding. The network is capable of performing a prediction for a single ECU, meaning that for a set of ECUs the prediction is calculated for each one separately. The input features were chosen to be the WCET, the deadline, the priority (as a potential extension for other types of task sets and schedulers) and the number of planned jobs for a maximum of 8 tasks per ECU, while 20 output neurons produced individual probability predictions, whose values were then averaged for the final prediction. After the training with 4500 samples and testing with 1500 samples, its accuracy showed to be 0.85. While this is far from a perfect result, the SNN allowed for testing the task distribution. Also, in future work, with a more extensive data set this performance could be improved.

At the next stage of the analysis, the ECUs and the SNN were further integrated with the deployment tool to show that it was capable of predicting feasible task distributions at runtime, deploying them to the ECUs and reacting to different situations, such as a task set missing a deadline, the arrival of new tasks, or even a sudden failure of an ECU. To achieve this, the deployment tool calculates task distributions that deviate as little as possible from the current distribution in order to create the next safe system state without interfering too much with the executing tasks through unnecessary migrations. Therefore, even before deadlines are missed, the deployment tool generates such possible task distributions and hands them to the machine learning component to predict the schedulability percentages for each of them. In the event of a deadline miss the most promising task distribution is selected and carried out, triggering a task migration. In the event of a change in the set of tasks to be executed or the set of ECUs available, new possible distributions are generated to fit them all. In the tests carried out, the process was found to take between 40 and 45 seconds, divided in the following way: around 40 seconds for starting and stopping the SNN on the SpiNNaker, around 1 second for executing it and collecting the predictions, a maximum of 1 second for the communication between tool and ECUs and around 100 ms for starting and stopping the tasks on each ECU.

As this is unfortunately too slow to predict the task set distributions in real-time, in particular due to the slow startup process in the SpiNNaker, we assume that the decoupling of the task planning with already prepared task distribution lists in case of a needed migration will mitigate this problem, as well as the enhancement of this first approach for a Spiking Neural Network as an ML component. Also, other ML algorithms investigated at the chair have shown that their prediction time might be suitable for real-time deployments, but they are still subject to further research, which is currently being performed and is planned to be published in the future.

The deployment system developed allowed for distributing any combination of task sets to the ECUs and confirming the feasibility of the schedule, which can be used for improving the schedulability analysis algorithm. The use of an EDF scheduler allowed for reaching very high utilization values with different task combinations, resulting in more than 98% of the task sets with a total utilization smaller or equal to 0.95 being successful, without taking into account the implementation overhead for EDF and deployment tasks in an ECU. However, sometimes task sets with a total utilization greater than 1.0 were reported as successful, as no deadlines were missed, even when not including the autonomous task. This occurred likely because of the large variation in periods between different tasks, as some tasks could finish executing their jobs before tasks with larger periods would cause a missed deadline, or because of variations in the WCET, like in the case of the autonomous task. Another possible reason for this behavior is the fact that the deployment tool would often trigger new task distributions before all tasks finished their jobs, causing running task sets to be interrupted prematurely. This is because the deployment tool continuously performs schedulability analysis for different distributions, picking the one that is least likely to fail. This deployment was tested with only 3 ECUs, but could be extended to any number of devices, and we are considering extending the setup to 10 devices for further research.

In regard to the autonomous task, it was able to fulfill its goal, and the robot could find the exit to the labyrinth, even with the changes in the task board configurations. However, when the machine-learning-based schedulability analysis predicted a better configuration that involved moving the task to another board, it would have to start from the beginning. This is the expected behavior, as the processed data is stored locally, but is a limitation worth noting, as in these cases, the robot must restart the pathfinding process, which might result in first going back to previously explored zones of the map, and then a longer search. It is also worth noting that the visual feedback provided in the simulated environment made it possible to notice when the board executing the autonomous task is overloaded, as this task responds more slowly, often resulting in the robot bumping into obstacles.

div.head: VII. DISCUSSION
div.p: This is the first approach at our research group at integrating the machine-learning-based schedulability analysis with an architecture that exploits real-time concepts, especially by using an EDF scheduler. This type of scheduler assigns dynamic priorities to the tasks, as opposed to the fixedpriority approaches used before in our research, which makes it possible to always find a schedule for the tasks if any other kind of scheduler would find one, and is therefore commonly used in the development of real-time systems. This allows for further improvement and tailoring of the machine learning techniques to real automotive systems. Also, the change to this architecture permits testing tasks with shorter periods, which normally represent greater challenges as time for executing the task deployment and eventually the migration.

The introduction of the automatically generated dummy tasks helps improve the development process for further research, as it can provide us with a variety of tasks with reliable execution times and a range of execution times and periods. This would allow for potentially infinite configurations to generate training data and test the machine learning algorithms and deployment. Additionally, the autonomous task introduces a realistic task which allows for testing the task migration approach on conditions closer to those of a real car, where tasks might have more variation in the execution times and the resources used.

The data on whether the execution of the task sets was successful or not was collected by the deployment tasks in the ECUs and the central deployment tool, which permitted the collection of data for training the different machine learning algorithms with real execution data. Prior to this, training data available at our research group were based on a system that had limitations for exploiting real-time concepts, and so the collection of new data is essential for ensuring the results collected from applying these techniques are relevant.

However, this development presented some shortcomings and has to be completed and improved in future work. First of all, the execution of the task migration has to be implemented, as in this paper the tasks are just started or stopped at different devices, but they are not migrated with context. It is especially necessary to consider cases where tasks are interrupted in the middle of the execution of a job or where data from previous jobs is relevant for execution, such as the case of the autonomous task described in this paper. Also, up to now, the execution of the jobs has been implemented with time relative to the executing ECU, neglecting time spent during the communication for the deployment of the tasks or the actual execution of the migration. It is a planned improvement for the development to bound the communication times and establish a time synchronization protocol, as it is important to ensure deadlines are actually met. It would also be of interest to investigate how phase changes affect the schedulability of a task set.

The exploitation of the multi-core functionality in the devices will help achieving higher utilization values and testing the approach to schedulability analysis on devices with higher performance capabilities. While the general architecture presented here is extendable to multi-core systems, some elements may have to be adapted, such as the scheduling process and the generation of task distributions.

Additionally, in our current implementation all tasks are compiled with the main system, reducing scalability for larger numbers of complex tasks. For this reason, it would be interesting to explore the actual deployment of task binaries that need to be executed on a board, so that tasks that are not relevant to a given board should not need to be stored there. This could probably also allow a wider range of applications, such as updates applied only to a central unit.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: ECU consolidation is expected to play a big role in the future of the automotive industry, especially in terms of cost optimization. To achieve this, task migration can be used to reduce the need for task-specific devices in the car. The work documented in this paper provides a development platform that will allow the further development of task migration approaches. In particular, even though the platform needs further improvement in some areas, it serves as a baseline for evaluating the real-time concepts involved in real automotive tasks. Also, it provides the opportunity of collecting realtime relevant training data for the machine learning algorithms investigated in our research. These contributions set an additional milestone on our approach to ECU consolidation through the application of machine-learning-based schedulability analysis.

As this paper focuses on the developed architecture, the deployment tool and the different machine learning algorithms under development, including the spiking neural network approach, are not explored extensively. We are planning to cover these topics and the multi-core extension of the architecture in future publications.
